entry.title: Bread, butter and a WhatsApp prescription

link.title: Bread, butter and a WhatsApp prescription

entry.content:
“Of course, we cannot give bread and butter for all 6000 patients. But we gave provisions for about 300 of them through various sources.” A manager heading outreach at the Schizophrenia Research Foundation, Chennai, on the months after India's 2020 lockdown

That sentence is from an interview with a service provider at the Schizophrenia Research Foundation (SCARF), a non-government organisation in Chennai that provides care for a range of mental disorders and runs outreach services for rural communities. It is an odd thing to hear from a mental health organisation, because food is not usually counted as part of mental health care. But the paper places it in a section on the burden of care at home, where the closure of the vocational centre and day-care came on top of job loss, pay cuts and rising debt for caregivers. In that situation the two could not really be separated, and the people interviewed did not try to separate them.

This post is about my first research paper, The COVID-19 pandemic and its impact on mental health services: the provider perspective, published in the Journal of Public Health in October 2021 . It came out of a partnership between LEAD at Krea University and the University of Oxford, funded through the Global Challenges Research Fund’s India–Oxford Initiative, and it asked a fairly simple question: when the country shut down, what happened to community mental health services, and how did the people providing them keep them running?

I should say up front what my part in it was. The interviews, the focus group and the thematic analysis were done by my co-authors. My part was the literature review, which meant reading what had been reported from a geographically and socio-economically spread set of countries and using it to place the Chennai data in a wider context. The journal format is tight, about six pages, and most of the participants’ words had to be cut down to fragments. So, five years on, I wanted to write about it in a form where the quotes get more room and some of the numbers can be drawn out.

The view from outside

By late 2020 it was already clear that mental health care had been hit hard almost everywhere. In October 2020 the World Health Organization published a survey of 130 countries , and the headline figure was blunt.

The literature I was reading at the time came at the problem from several directions. From China there were accounts of psychiatric hospitals reorganising themselves around infection control . From the United States, descriptions of how psychiatric care had been reshaped in the first months . From the UK, a mixed-methods study of services for older adults , and from a cross-continental group, lessons on managing psychiatric conditions during the pandemic . A piece in The Lancet Psychiatry set out how mental health care should change as a consequence . In India, services were disrupted by the nationwide lockdown in March 2020, and the government released guidelines to move to telemedicine . Tele-psychiatry had raised concerns about patient dynamics, proper diagnosis and legal issues , though it had worked in some contexts .

What most of this work described was disruption: what stopped, what moved online, which systems were under strain. There was much less on how the organisations doing the care actually adapted, and that gap matters more in India than in many of the countries above, because mental health outreach to communities and vulnerable groups here was pioneered by NGOs, and their lessons have proved useful to the public mental health system . So the study went to the people who had kept care going, and asked them.

One organisation, many services

SCARF is, in the paper’s words, a training centre for psychiatry, psychology and psychiatric social work, and a training partner for public mental health services, as well as a provider . That breadth was useful: it meant one organisation could stand in for many kinds of service at once, from inpatient wards to rural outreach.

The people interviewed included managers of clinical services, administrative staff, psychiatrists, social workers, a psychologist and research staff, with between three and more than twenty years at the organisation. Their accounts covered the period from February to December 2020, and the fieldwork itself ran over December 2020 and January 2021.

What broke

The first thing to go was access. For two weeks of complete lockdown everything stopped, and even once essential services resumed, patients could not easily reach the centre. Not every neighbourhood pharmacy stocked psychiatric medication, and some pharmacists that did were reluctant to dispense it. In smaller towns, psychiatric care was taken over for COVID-19 treatment. Rural patients were stopped by the police and fined on their way to refill prescriptions at SCARF, even when they showed the prescription.

“These are people who can’t even afford medicines… it felt painful that we were helpless.” A manager heading outreach efforts (P6)

Missed medication meant relapses of conditions like schizophrenia and mood disorders, often needing in-patient care, at exactly the time the centre had stopped admissions for fear of spreading COVID-19 inside the facility. One of the psychiatrists recalled handling “at least ten DESPERATE requests for admissions” (the capitals are in the transcript). For patients who had been discharged and rehabilitated, the closure of the vocational centre took away a daily routine as well; the same psychiatrist described the “11 o clock tea” and the people they talked to, and said: “It was sad for them because this was their social life…”

The providers were affected as well. The paper has a section on their personal costs, which I think is easy to skim past and should not be. Work moved onto personal phones and into the time that used to belong to families. One counsellor, taking sessions from home, said that her children “would wonder why the person on the other end was crying so much”.

What they built instead

What I find most striking, reading the paper again, is how ordinary the adaptations were. Prescriptions were written on the official pad, signed, photographed and sent over WhatsApp, in line with the teleconsultation guidelines, and the consultants then spent time on the phone with pharmacists sorting out legibility, brand names and substitutes. A health worker tracked down the doctors of clients stuck in other districts and passed their prescriptions along.

A 24-hour helpline, advertised by the government, linked new and existing patients to consultants and therapists, and stretched everyone’s working hours. In the in-patient centres, staff used their own phones to set up video calls with families, because many patients did not have smartphones. Even the paperwork needed a person: when staff or patients with cards and e-passes were stopped, the police would be handed a phone with an administrator on the other end. Much of the coordination itself happened in WhatsApp groups.

The clearest change in clinical practice was time. One psychiatrist described how a first consultation for a new patient, which used to take an hour, was now done in fifteen to twenty minutes.

A natural reading of that number is that care got worse. I do not think the paper lets us say that, and I would be wary of saying it here. The time in the room shrank, but the work was redistributed: the history was taken over the phone before the visit, and a case worker followed up afterwards. Whether that amounted to a loss, a different kind of care, or in some cases a better use of a psychiatrist’s hour is something interviews with providers alone cannot settle.

Telemedicine is where the trade-offs were clearest. The paper’s abstract says it enabled an expansion of both the service and its clientele, as well as efficiency. It also changed what a therapy session was like, for both sides: some clients took phone sessions as “a friendly catch-up call rather than a teletherapy session”.

The phrase “casualization” is the one I keep coming back to.The abstract uses "casualization of therapy"; the discussion uses "casualization of the exchange between service provider and patient". I have used both, since they describe the same concern from slightly different angles. A therapy session in a clinic has a frame around it: a room, a time, a journey to get there. Over the phone, that frame dissolves into the rest of the day, and some patients, reasonably enough, treated it like any other call. I doubt better connectivity would have fixed that.

Relationships, responsiveness, resilience

When the paper pulls these threads together, it names “three crucial elements in continuity and quality service delivery: relationships, responsiveness and resilience” .

I think the useful thing about this framing is that none of the three is a technology or a policy. They are properties of an organisation that existed before the pandemic and were tested by it. The relationships had been built over many years, partly through educating patients and families, and the providers felt that psycho-education showed its value in how well patients kept to treatment. The resilience drew on lessons from earlier floods, a tsunami and cyclones, and on prior experience with tele-psychiatry. The WhatsApp prescription only works if the health worker already knows the patient’s doctor, and provisions only reach 300 patients if somebody already knows who those patients are. In that sense SCARF is a single, fairly small test case of a broader question that the national-level surveys could not get at: what is it, inside an organisation, that lets care continue when the system around it stops?

What this study cannot tell us

The paper is direct about its main limitation: “Though limited to a single NGO and to providers, insights from a variety of services within mental healthcare was gleaned” . Both halves of that sentence matter. One organisation in one city, however broad its services, is not Indian community mental health care as a whole. And the people we heard from were the people delivering care, not receiving it. We do not know how the shortened consultation felt from the patient’s side, whether the phone sessions that providers worried were too casual felt that way to the people on the other end, or what the families who were not among the 300 made of the year.

It is also a retrospective account. The interviews were conducted at the end of 2020 about the months that came before, and what people remember of a crisis, and how they make sense of it afterwards, is not quite the same as what happened at the time. None of this undermines the findings, but it does bound them, and I would rather say so plainly than have the post read as a claim about more than it is.

Coming back to it

The paper ends by arguing that these insights are crucial for planning resilient community-based mental health care, and the wider literature at the time was saying something similar: that the pandemic was an opportunity to reform mental health care in India , and that health systems needed to be built with preparedness in mind . The paper is specific about what that would mean: bringing care for people with mental illness into government and city disaster planning, including housing, transport and medication; sensitising the police and other enforcing authorities to their needs; training health workers for isolation, infection and relocation; and preparing patients and caregivers for how to manage care during a disaster.

Reading it again now, the questions I am left with are ones the study opened rather than answered. Which of these adaptations outlasted the pandemic? Did the phone intake before a consultation become routine, and if it did, did anyone check what it changed for patients? If relationships with communities were what made continuity possible, can that be planned for, or only maintained? And how would you even measure a relationship as a piece of health infrastructure, in a way that would make it visible to the people who fund and plan services? I do not have answers to these, and I suspect they need the patient and family perspective that this study did not have.

It was my first time seeing my name on a paper, and I am properly thankful to my co-authors, Sapna Nair, Preethi Kannan, Ananya Raju, John Mathew and Padmavati Ramachandran, for bringing me in, and to the providers at SCARF who gave their time to be interviewed at the end of a very hard year. The full paper is available from the Journal of Public Health.
entry.summary: How one community mental health organisation in Chennai kept care going through the 2020 lockdown. A visual walk through my first research paper, published in the Journal of Public Health.

entry.title: a post with plotly.js
entry.content:
This is an example post with some plotly code.

```plotly
{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "type": "scatter"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "type": "scatter"
    }
  ]
}
```

Which generates:

{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "type": "scatter"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "type": "scatter"
    }
  ]
}

Also another example chart.

```plotly
{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "mode": "markers"
    },
    {
      "x": [2, 3, 4, 5],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "mode": "lines"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [12, 9, 15, 12],
      "mode": "lines+markers"
    }
  ],
  "layout": {
    "title": {
      "text": "Line and Scatter Plot"
    }
  }
}
```

This is how it looks like:

{
  "data": [
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [10, 15, 13, 17],
      "mode": "markers"
    },
    {
      "x": [2, 3, 4, 5],
      "y": [16, 5, 11, 9],
      "mode": "lines"
    },
    {
      "x": [1, 2, 3, 4],
      "y": [12, 9, 15, 12],
      "mode": "lines+markers"
    }
  ],
  "layout": {
    "title": {
      "text": "Line and Scatter Plot"
    }
  }
}

entry.title: a post with tabs
entry.content:
This is how a post with tabs looks like. Note that the tabs could be used for different purposes, not only for code.

First tabs

To add tabs, use the following syntax:

{% tabs group-name %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-1 %}

Content 1

{% endtab %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-2 %}

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}

With this you can generate visualizations like:

  • php
  • js
  • ruby 
  • var_dump('hello');

  • console.log("hello");

  • pputs 'hello'

Another example

  • yaml
  • json 
  • hello:
  - "whatsup"
  - "hi"

  • {
  "hello": ["whatsup", "hi"]
}

Tabs for something else

  • text
  • quote
  • list

  • Regular text

  • A quote

  • Hipster list

    • brunch
    • fixie
    • raybans
    • messenger bag

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Generates:

% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

entry.title: a post with code diff
entry.content:
You can display diff code by using the regular markdown syntax:

```diff
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

Which generates:

diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")

But this is difficult to read, specially if you have a large diff. You can use diff2html to display a more readable version of the diff. For this, just use diff2html instead of diff for the code block language:

```diff2html
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

entry.title: a post with vega lite
entry.content:
This is an example post with some vega lite code.

```vega_lite
{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A dot plot showing each movie in the database, and the difference from the average movie rating. The display is sorted by year to visualize everything in sequential order. The graph is for all Movies before 2019.",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega/main/docs/data/movies.json"
  },
  "transform": [
    {"filter": "datum['IMDB Rating'] != null"},
    {"filter": {"timeUnit": "year", "field": "Release Date", "range": [null, 2019]}},
    {
      "joinaggregate": [{
        "op": "mean",
        "field": "IMDB Rating",
        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "scale": {"domainMid": 0},
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    }
  }
}
```

Which generates:

{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A dot plot showing each movie in the database, and the difference from the average movie rating. The display is sorted by year to visualize everything in sequential order. The graph is for all Movies before 2019.",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega/main/docs/data/movies.json"
  },
  "transform": [
    {"filter": "datum['IMDB Rating'] != null"},
    {"filter": {"timeUnit": "year", "field": "Release Date", "range": [null, 2019]}},
    {
      "joinaggregate": [{
        "op": "mean",
        "field": "IMDB Rating",
        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "scale": {"domainMid": 0},
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    }
  }
}

This plot supports both light and dark themes.
